title: The Boundaries of Class: imaginary quadratic class numbers from class number one to 3500, kernel-checked where possible
description:
The Boundaries of Class collects one line of work on the class numbers of imaginary quadratic fields, from class number one up to class number 3500. It builds on the arguments against Landau–Siegel zeros that appeared in October 2026, chiefly OpenAI's Lean-formalized zero-free region Re s > 7/8 for Dirichlet L-functions. It began as an entry for Terence Tao's tenth-discriminant challenge of 20 October 2026. Each entry states exactly what a machine has checked and what it has not.

The six entries (each with its own paper in the archive):

  1. Class number one, first route (kernel-checked). For squarefree m ≥ 1, Q(√−m) has class number one if and only if m ∈ {1, 2, 3, 7, 11, 19, 43, 67, 163}. The proof uses no Heegner, Baker, Stark or Gross–Zagier input. OpenAI's 7/8 theorem and the Chowla–Selberg formula give d ≤ 652, and split-prime certificates settle the rest.
  2. Class number one, determinant route (kernel-checked). The same theorem, with no L-function, zeta function or zero-free theorem in its closure. It uses Green's derivative determinant, made nonzero by van Dijk's finite-field argument, following the companion note of twinheterodox/tenth-discriminant.
  3. Class number at most two (kernel-checked). Exactly 27 fields have class number at most two, and exactly eighteen have class number two. This is LemmaLab's class-sum extension of the first route.
  4. Tenth-discriminant bounds compared (not kernel-checked; certified in ball arithmetic). It surveys the bounds posted in the challenge thread and puts them on one scale. It also improves the light-machinery determinant bound to the cutoff |D| < 548 for class number one.
  5. Two-sided bounds for every field (kernel-checked; 28 Lean statements). With d = |disc K|:
    • h ≥ (1/3)√d/log d for d ≥ 2981, and h ≥ d^{7/16}/17 for d ≥ 1000;
    • Dirichlet's class number formula, and h ≤ (1/π)√d(log d + 7/6);
    • ten explicit thresholds and three point values, including d ≥ 2^40 ⇒ h ≥ 17,450.
    The 7/8 theorem is used at real points only.
  6. Class number at most 3500 (not kernel-checked as a whole). Assuming the explicit real-zero bound of Kimura's Theorem 1, exactly 50,299,869 fields have class number at most 3500; the largest |D| is 3,495,584,467 (h = 3477). It extends Jaswal's classification by his method, reproduces his and Kimura's lists exactly, and was re-implemented and cross-checked independently. The full list is included in this record.

How it was checked. Every Lean statement uses only Mathlib's definitions and depends only on the three standard axioms. Comparator accepts the proofs under two independent kernels, Lean's and nanoda. The runs were local and not sandboxed. Where OpenAI's 7/8 theorem is used, its Lean proof is inside the checked closure rather than assumed; its manuscript is not refereed. Entries 4 and 6 rest on interval arithmetic and on agreement between independent programs and published data, and say so. None of this work has been refereed.

This version (2.0.1) corrects two bibliographic references. Version 2.0.0 renamed the repository (formerly tenth-discriminant) and added entries 5 and 6. The mathematics, code and data are unchanged from 2.0.0.

Credits. The challenge is Tao's. The arguments excluding Siegel zeros are OpenAI's, with further proofs by Banks, Kerr and Green. The explicit zero gap is Kimura's, and the method for h ≤ 3000 is Jaswal's. The routes from the challenge thread are credited comment by comment in the papers.

AI disclosure. The work was produced with extensive use of Claude (Anthropic) under the author's direction, and a separate AI session reviewed each step. That review is not a substitute for a human referee.
